summary: Seaforth Bank is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for production LLM inference. Primary drivers are data isolation, predictable latency, and cost control. They want reserved GPU pools with burst capacity for month-end spikes. Key concerns: network peering/VPC setup, KMS/HSM integration, audit logs, and predictable throughput. Timeline: pilot in early March, decision by end of Q2.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~52 min | Recording: yes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Marco Liu (Redwood SE), Nina Roberts (Seaforth CTO), Aaron Kim (Head of ML), Laila Hassan (Infra Lead)

00:00 Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear us OK?
00:03 Nina: Yep can hear, thanks. We kicked off late but all good.
00:08 Sofia: Great. Quick agenda - we're here to understand your production needs for an LLM infra, go over Dedicated offering, and figure out next steps for a pilot. Marco will cover technical details.
00:20 Marco: Hi all - quick intro from me, I'm Marco in solutions engineering, I'll go deep on GPU pools, autoscale, and network.
00:28 Aaron: Thanks. For context - our team runs a document understanding pipeline, two models: a 7B fine-tuned for extraction and a 13B for synthesis. Today it's on-prem with GPUs, but the infra is brittle. We're exploring Redwood so we can get predictable latency and better ops.
00:45 Laila: And we need strict data isolation - can't have multi-tenant access to models or transient storage. Also curious about burst for month-end processing - traffic can jump 6-8x for a few hours.
01:00 Marco: Understood. Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools for your account only, with options for private VPC peering. You get tenant isolation at the runtime level - networks, storage mounts, and logs are isolated.
01:12 Nina: Can you explain how burst works? We don't want to buy for peak all the time.
01:18 Marco: Sure. We support a base reserved capacity and a burst pool - burst can be configured as paid spare capacity or elastically allocated from lower-priority machines. You can set policies: maximum burst units, cost limits, and fallback rules (e.g., route to a cheaper quantized variant). Burst latency is slightly higher if provisioning from elastic nodes but still within typical SLOs.
01:40 Aaron: What about cold starts for burst? If we spin up GPUs will KV cache warm-up add latency?
01:46 Marco: Good question. We do a couple things: warm standby kernels for common models, and we recommend pre-warming KV cache for prefixes when you have predictable spike windows. There's also a hybrid approach - keep a small hot pool plus burst for scaling.
02:05 Laila: How are the GPUs reserved - by instance count or by vCPU/GPU sharing? We have procurement constraints around GPU SKUs.
02:12 Marco: Reservations are by GPU count and family (e.g., A100, H100) and you can pin to specific SKUs in Dedicated contracts. We also offer per-GPU throughput guarantees and telemetry for utilization.
02:25 Nina: We need KMS integration - customer-managed keys and HSM are a hard requirement.
02:30 Marco: We integrate with customer KMS providers and support HSM-backed key wrapping for model assets and logs. For Private deployments we can do on-prem HSM; for Dedicated we offer customer KMS via VPC-connected key endpoints. We'll share the integration guide.
02:44 Laila: Network setup - do you do VPC peering or private link? Our infra security team prefers peering and strict ACLs.
02:50 Marco: Both are supported. For Dedicated we commonly use VPC peering with route tables and security groups. We can also do PrivateLink for some cloud providers. We'll provide a reference architecture diagram.
03:05 Aaron: From ML side, we care about latency distribution - p95/p99. What numbers can we expect for gen responses on 13B?
03:12 Marco: For optimized kernels on H100 with continuous batching disabled for strict latency SLOs, p95 for 13B is in the 120-220ms per-token range depending on sequence length; p99 will be higher. For strict low-latency you can pin models to dedicated machines with lower batching and disable prefetching. We can run a benchmark with your seq lengths to produce real numbers.
03:35 Nina: Cost - can you give an example: if we reserve 8 H100s with a small hot pool and 8 H100 burst capacity, what's a ballpark monthly?
03:45 Sofia: We'll send an itemized pricing guide, but to ballpark - reserved capacity is a fixed monthly commit, burst is metered. Pricing varies by region and SKU; I'll follow up with concrete numbers.
03:58 Laila: SLA expectations? Uptime and latency SLOs?
04:02 Marco: We offer SLA-backed uptime for Dedicated and latency targets depending on config. Standard SLA is 99.9% availability; for stricter SLOs we do runbooked configs and can include performance SLAs in enterprise contracts.
04:17 Aaron: How does caching work - we need prefix and KV cache to reduce tokens and cost.
04:22 Marco: We provide automatic KV cache management and prefix caching; you can configure retention and sharding. It reduces per-token computation significantly for repeat prefixes. For multi-node setups we do cache synchronization strategies - eventual consistency for KV entries is typical, but you can pin to a single node if you require strict consistency.
04:45 Nina: Security audits - do you have SOC2, ISO docs, pen-testing reports?
04:50 Marco: Yes SOC2 Type II, ISO 27001 evidence available. We'll share redacted reports and a security questionnaire.
04:57 Laila: And how are logs/audit trails handled? We need per-request audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
05:02 Marco: We stream audit logs to your logging endpoint over TLS and can support structured per-token metadata. Logs are encrypted at rest with your KMS keys if requested.
05:14 Aaron: Integration with our model registry - we version models internally, how do rollouts work?
05:20 Marco: Redwood supports model pinning, canary rollouts and A/B configs. You can point routes to model versions and do gradual shifts. Rollbacks are supported as part of the control plane.
05:34 Nina: For the pilot - we want a 2-week pilot with a small reserved pool and burst enabled, run our traffic profile including month-end spike simulation. Is that doable?
05:42 Sofia: Absolutely. Typical pilot is 2-4 weeks. We'll provision a small Dedicated pool and help run the benchmark. After that we can propose a committed sizing.
05:50 Laila: Who on Redwood will handle the networking onboarding?
05:54 Sofia: Marco will own the technical onboarding with our infra ops team and coordinate with your network engineers.
06:00 Aaron: A few follow-ups - does Redwood support on-prem private deployment if we later want air-gapped?
06:06 Marco: Yes, Redwood Private is available as a customer-managed deployment; it requires additional ops engagement and licensing. For now Dedicated with VPC peering is the fastest path.
06:20 Nina: Any notable gotchas?
06:23 Marco: A couple - KV cache warm-up is important for burst windows, and network egress can add variability; also quantization and kernel selection trade quality vs cost. We'll help pick defaults based on your workload.
06:38 Sofia: OK, quick recap and next steps - we'll: 1) send pricing and contract template, 2) Marco will upload SOC2 and network diagram, 3) schedule pilot kickoff for 2026-03-10, 4) Seaforth to provide traffic profile and SLOs.
06:55 Nina: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
07:00 Sofia: Thanks all - we'll follow up via email with calendar invites and docs.

Notes: transcript includes occasional transcription artifacts - speaker overlap at 02:12 timestamp, and a few acronyms mis-captured (e.g., KV-cache sometimes transcribed as K-V cash).
